sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the type, colors, and shapes share one mood and era, so the piece reads as one whole rather than a collage?** No. The page uses three type voices that don't belong together. There's a fat brush script for "Crossing the river" (96–548, 125–215) and "Good to know" (850–1056, 175–220). There's a bookish serif for the grey subtitle (96, 215–280), the h2s and the box body. And there's a neutral UI sans for the nav, the main body and the button. The script brings a beach-café, 2010s-retro mood to a page that is otherwise calm, plain transport information. So the first thing the eye lands on is the one element that doesn't match the rest. The page reads as assembled from parts rather than designed as one thing, and the headline looks more decorative than trustworthy for timetable information. None of the catalog entries for this line has an approved source, so this rests on common sense. The fix is to cut to two families. Either use the serif for every heading and drop the script, or, if a river-holiday character is wanted, put it in one place, the h1 only, and set everything else in the serif and sans. Taste. Weight: major.
2. **Within one screen or image, does each kind of element look the same everywhere it appears?** No. There are two sets of section headings. "Good to know" is in script, while "When the boats run" (96–366, 320–348) and "Bicycles and luggage" (96–381, 475–503) are in serif. Body text is also split: the box body (849–1107, 235–410) is a larger serif, while the main-column paragraphs are sans. So headings of the same level and paragraphs of the same kind look like they come from two different designs. The box reads as if it were pasted in from another site, and the viewer gets no reliable cue for what a section heading or a paragraph looks like. Gerstner, *Designing Programmes* (elements of one kind follow one program), and Nielsen heuristic 4 (consistency and standards). The fix is to give the box heading the same style as the h2s and the box body the same face and size as the main body. Then only the box border and the button set the box apart. Convention. Weight: major. (It shares a root with finding 1, and the director may merge them.)
3. **Does each heading name what its section holds?** No. "Good to know" (850, 175–220) names no topic. The box is about where to find printed timetables and weekly changes, so a passenger scanning for "where do I check changes?" gets no hint from the heading. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.6 (headings describe topic or purpose). The fix is a heading that says what's inside, such as "Printed timetables and changes". Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.** The page's job is clear in one glance. The headline, the subtitle naming the exact route ("north landing to market quay") and two plainly named sections ("When the boats run", "Bicycles and luggage") tell a passenger what this is within seconds. The palette is quiet, with a neutral grey, white and one blue for the single action. That suits practical travel information and keeps the button as the only colored element on the page.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 5 yes, 3 no (type, colors and shapes share one mood and era; each kind of element looks the same everywhere; each heading names what its section holds), 0 unsure

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No. There are two problems here.
   - **The sidebar outranks the main content.** "Good to know" (about x 849–1055, y 175–220) is set in the same brush script as the page title, at about 44 px. That makes it the second-loudest element on the page, larger and more decorative than the main section headings "When the boats run" and "Bicycles and luggage" (about 28 px bold serif, y 320–345 and 475–500). The sidebar body (about 20 px serif) is also larger than the main body (about 18 px Inter). So after the title, the eye jumps to the aside before the content. The aside reads as a second title rather than a side note, and the page seems to have two starting points.
   - **The subtitle and the H2s are close in size.** The grey subtitle "A short guide for passengers…" (about 24 px regular serif) and the H2s (about 28 px bold serif) use the same serif and are only about 4 px apart. Weight and colour separate them, so they don't merge. But the serif is used at two near sizes, and the sidebar body adds a third serif size at about 20 px. With the 18 px sans body, that gives four or five text sizes in the 18–28 px band, which looks picked one at a time rather than drawn from a scale (Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1 "Don't compose without a scale").

   **Direction of the fix:** Keep the script for the page title only. Set "Good to know" as a sidebar heading at or below the H2 level, for example the H2 serif at a smaller size. Set the sidebar body at the main body size, or smaller. Tighten the scale to title / H2 / body, plus one subtitle size that is clearly apart from the H2: either clearly larger, or the body size in grey.

   Marked as a **defect** (the aside competes with the main content for second place) and a **convention** (Bringhurst on the scale). Weight: **minor**. The page is short, and the reader still finds the title and both sections. The fix mainly stops the aside pulling the eye away, and makes the page look deliberate.

**What's working.**
- **The title clearly leads.** "Crossing the river" is far larger than anything else, so the eye knows where to start.
- **Headings differ from body on more than size.** The H2s are bold serif and the body is regular sans, so each section starts obviously, with no risk of a heading reading as a paragraph (Dair's contrast of form and weight).

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (each level of the text distinct, no two sizes almost the same)

I've finished checking the arrangement section; here is the report.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do all blocks, pictures included, take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid, so column lines and gutters repeat down the page?** No.
   - **Where:** The left side follows a clear line: the logo, H1, subtitle, both H2s and the body text all start at x≈96. The right side follows nothing. The "Good to know" card runs from x≈820 to x≈1149, but the nav ends at x≈1184, so the card's right edge matches no other edge on the page. The gap between the main text (ends at x≈740) and the card is about 80 px, and the right margin (≈130 px) is not the same as the left margin (96 px).
   - **What the viewer sees:** The card looks placed by eye. It floats about 35 px inside the line the nav sets, and the page's right side feels loose next to its tight left side.
   - **Why:** Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, and Samara, *Making and Breaking the Grid*: when a block's edges match no other block, it reads as placed by eye.
   - **Fix:** Put the card on the same column structure as the header, so its right edge meets the nav's right edge at ~1184. Size the gutter from the same interval the page uses elsewhere.
   - **Kind and weight:** Convention. Minor.
2. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?** No.
   - **Where:** Two near-misses. The card's top border (y≈146) sits just below the H1's cap height (y≈133), so it is almost aligned with the headline but not quite. The card's right edge falls about 35 px short of the nav's right edge (finding 1).
   - **What the viewer sees:** Both edges look like they were meant to line up and missed, so the top of the page looks a little unfinished.
   - **Why:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance": a placement that is neither clearly here nor clearly there makes the eye waver.
   - **Fix:** Commit either way. Align the card top exactly with the H1's top or cap height, or drop the card clearly below it (for example, level with the subtitle or the first H2) so the offset reads as a choice.
   - **Kind and weight:** Convention. Minor.
3. **Do lines of text in neighboring columns sit on the same baselines?** No.
   - **Where:** The card's body lines step about 30 px apart (rows near y≈246, 276, 306, 336, 366, 396). The main body steps about 27 px (y≈375, 402, 429). Where the two columns sit side by side (y≈330–480), their lines do not form straight rows across the gap.
   - **What the viewer sees:** Barely noticeable, because the card is a boxed aside and not a parallel text column. The two columns simply run on unrelated rhythms.
   - **Why:** Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "Construction of the grid".
   - **Fix:** Optional here. Share one baseline step (one line-height unit) between the main text and the card if the page is meant to feel built to a grid.
   - **Kind and weight:** Convention. Minor.

**What's working.**
- **Spacing within and between sections:** Each H2 sits about 10 px above its paragraph and about 40 px below the paragraph before it. "When the boats run" and "Bicycles and luggage" therefore read as two clear units with no effort.
- **The card as one group:** The card holds one group only (heading, note, and its one button) and it is placed off-centre. The page reads as main content plus an aside, and the eye moves from the H1 through the sections to the card's button with nothing pulling it off the page.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 10 yes, 3 no (one grid governs edges and gutters; exact alignment with no near-misses; baselines across columns), 0 unsure

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the typefaces follow one plan, one family or a few plainly different faces, with no face that nearly matches another and no extra unrelated face?** No. The page uses three unrelated kinds of type:
   - A brush script for "Crossing the river" (about x 96–545, y 125–215) and "Good to know" (about x 849–1055, y 175–220).
   - A serif for the subtitle, the two section headings and the sidebar paragraph.
   - A sans serif for the nav, the main paragraphs and the button.

   The roles also cross over: running text is sans in the main column (y 365–595) and serif in the sidebar (y 235–410). The reader sees two kinds of body copy and may take the sidebar for a different kind of content, such as a pulled quote or a notice, rather than more of the same guide. The script gives a timetable page a party-invitation tone, and that weakens its sense of reliability. Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 7–8: faces should agree or contrast with clear roles; a mix of unrelated faces sets up no relationship. Fix: give each face one job. One body face for all running text, sidebar included. One heading face. Keep the script, if at all, only for the one h1 as a deliberate accent, or drop it. Convention (Dair), plus taste on the script's tone. Weight: major.
2. **Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters?** No, in the sidebar. The "Printed timetables…" paragraph (x 849–1110, y 235–410) is set in serif at about 20 px in a column holding only 16–27 characters per line. That makes six lines out of one sentence, and the eye keeps jumping back to the left edge. The main-column paragraphs are fine at about 65–70 characters. Bringhurst, *Elements*, §2.1.2. Fix: set the sidebar text smaller, about the main body size or a step below, or widen the card, so lines reach about 35–45 characters. Convention. Weight: minor.
3. **Does the space between lines of a paragraph suit its line length, neither cramped nor so loose that the lines drift apart?** No, in the sidebar. The lines look to be spaced about 30 px apart on about 20 px type in that very short measure, so they read as separate strips rather than a block. Bringhurst §2.2.1 and Hochuli, *Detail in Typography* p. 47: shorter lines need less leading. Fix: tighten the sidebar leading to about 1.3–1.4, or fix the measure as in finding 2 and match the main body's leading. Convention. Weight: minor.
4. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line and no heading at the foot of a column?** No. "week." sits alone on the last line of the sidebar paragraph (about x 849–905, y 385–410). It leaves a short leftover line and adds a sixth line to a box that is already tall. Bringhurst §2.4.2. Fix: rewrapping per finding 2 will probably cure it. If not, keep the last two words together. Convention. Weight: minor.
5. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** No, borderline. The subtitle breaks "…on the north landing to / market quay route." (y 215–280), which strands "to" at the line end and splits the route's start and end across lines. The reader takes in "north landing to" as a unit before finding where it goes. No approved source covers breaks in headings, so this is common sense. Fix: break before "to", or reword so that "north landing to market quay" stays on one line. Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- Main-column body text is a plain sans at about 18 px with lines of about 65–70 characters and comfortable leading. It is a sound reading setting, slightly larger than the nav text, as it should be.
- The text is cut into small chunks under plain, verb-led headings ("When the boats run", "Bicycles and luggage"), so a passenger can scan straight to their question.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 25 yes, 5 no (typefaces follow one plan; lines of 45 to 75 characters; space between lines; clean breaks with no runt; headings break at phrase boundaries), 0 unsure

**First read (working notes).** The eye goes first to the large black script heading "Crossing the river", then to the grey serif subtitle, then across to the "Good to know" card and its blue button. It reads as a calm, plain information page for ferry passengers. The colour is quiet: near-black on white, with one blue.

**Job (assumed).** A page that tells ferry passengers how the crossing works and points them to the timetable.

**Walk: Color**
- Small palette, one neutral range plus one or two hues: yes. Near-black, a mid grey, a light grey for rules and borders, and one blue.
- Strong colour kept to a small area: yes. The only saturated colour is the blue button at about 849–1025 × 432–476.
- Clear range of light and dark, structure visible in greyscale: yes.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. There is no warm colour. The blue button is the one thing coloured, and blue is the usual colour for an action, so a cool colour coming forward helps this page.
- Matching colours look the same everywhere: yes.
- Neighbouring strong colours differ in lightness: yes. White on blue only.
- Status colours used only for their usual meaning: yes. Blue means an action.
- Meaning not carried by colour alone: yes. The button reads as a button from its shape and label as well as its colour.
- Dark theme not pure black: yes. The page is not a dark theme.

Every line is yes, so I did not open any entries.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Only one colour on the page.** Everything except the "See the timetable" button is a neutral, so the button is the only coloured thing there. The eye finds the page's one action without any extra weight or size, and it doesn't compete with the heading.
- **Structure comes from greys, not hues.** The near-black headings and body, the mid-grey subtitle and the pale card border and header rule give three clear levels of lightness. The page reads the same in greyscale, and the grey subtitle steps back from the heading without needing a second hue.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
The interface section applies but has no failures. The page has one primary button, nav links and no other controls. The image is 1280×800, which is about one screen, so I worked from the whole image.

**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has a header nav with three text links, a wordmark, and one filled button, "See the timetable". There are no forms, dialogs or other controls.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One clear primary action.** "See the timetable" (about x 849–1025, y 432–476) is the only filled control on the page. It is solid blue with bold white text, so it reads clearly as something to press. Every other action is a plain text link set lower. The button is about 176×44 px, well above the 24 px web minimum (WCAG 2.5.8). It sits right under the copy about printed timetables, so the next step is in front of the reader where they need it.
- **Conventional navigation.** The wordmark is top left and three short nav items sit top right ("Timetable", "Fares", "Landings"), above a thin rule. Visitors already know this layout from other sites, so it needs no learning (Jakob's law, Nielsen Norman Group). The labels are the passenger's own words, not internal terms. The nav links are spaced about 30 px apart, so each is easy to hit.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **Focus indicators.** Check in a browser whether the nav links and the button show a focus ring at least 2 px thick with 3:1 contrast. The button's dark-blue fill would hide a default blue ring, so it needs its own visible outline (WCAG 2.4.7 / 2.4.13).
- **Sticky header.** If the header stays fixed on scroll, check that it never covers a focused link or the button (WCAG 2.4.11).

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 31 yes, 0 no, 2 unsure (focus indicator 2 px at 3:1; focused control not covered by a sticky header)
